sections.title: What senior engineering judgment looks like
sections.deck: Michael Novati's rapid rise at Facebook becomes a conversation about impact, the limits of individual coding output, apprenticeship, AI, and how interviews try to recognize judgment.

blocks.question: How did you move from intern to principal-level E7 at Meta in six years?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati attributes his pace to giving Facebook an unusual amount of attention because he believed in its vision and wanted to increase its impact. He says compensation and promotion checklists were not his main motivation; seeing the work's effects created momentum that made him want to contribute more. He also emphasizes that the transitions between levels differ, so his path should not be reduced to a universal promotion recipe.

evidence.label: From intern to E7

followups.question: Which transition was the most difficult?
answer: He names E6 to E7. The move had no clear template for him: he was producing broader impact than most E6 engineers, but did not fit the company's familiar senior-engineer archetypes. He needed executive support to make the case for the level.

evidence.label: The E6-to-E7 transition

blocks.question: Does skipping meetings and working independently offer a general strategy for career growth?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati says he would not recommend opting out as a blanket tactic. His decision depended on the company's stated values and whether he was using the time for work with greater value. Sometimes he briefed a product manager beforehand so that person could represent his update or concern in the meeting. In his account, he was trying to avoid the time cost of a meeting, not to abandon the decision or the people involved.

evidence.label: Choosing which meetings to attend

blocks.question: How can a high-output individual contributor create impact across teams, and where does a coding-focused path reach its limits?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: The host asks how a person who writes most of the code alone can still have broad organizational impact. Novati agrees that one person has a limit: coding volume can make someone highly valuable, but influence across a larger group requires more than personal output. He describes receiving feedback that he needed to broaden his influence to reach the next level. In response, he organized a code-health summit that brought engineers from different migration and infrastructure efforts together. The work earned a stronger review and a path toward E8, but he realized that broader leadership was not the work he wanted most. He preferred writing code, shipping quickly, and seeing people use the result.
The interview keeps both sides of the tradeoff visible: a coding-machine identity can produce deep craft and fast delivery, while a higher level may require helping other people do better work.

evidence.label: Code volume, influence, and career fit

followups.question: Does company size change the amount of influence expected?
answer: Novati connects the expectation to Facebook's growth from roughly 200 engineers when he joined to thousands when he left. As the organization expanded, feedback increasingly asked him to influence through writing, leadership, and work across groups. He contrasts that with executive roles, whose decisions can affect thousands of engineers, and sees a ceiling on the number of people one individual contributor can reach alone.

evidence.label: Influence as the company grows

followups.question: Can very senior individual contributors still write code?
answer: Novati says a small number of very senior ICs do write code, but their standing is often associated with making other engineers better or untangling difficult, consequential problems rather than with raw code volume. One example he gives is a specialist who writes very little but can identify a crucial point in a complicated system.

evidence.label: Senior IC impact

blocks.question: Does AI make the high-volume coding path obsolete?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati says AI is changing the relationship between engineers and code quickly, and he does not claim to know the final shape of the work. At the time of the interview, he sees junior engineers using AI to produce much more code, while experienced engineers can direct agents because they already understand the codebase and what should be built. AI also makes some old rules about repetition and code volume less settled, though maintainability and performance still matter. For him, AI removes typing as a bottleneck: he reports that his own commit volume rose after the models became useful, because he could describe an implementation and let a model generate it.
His account is a time-bound observation. He is more interested in watching the change than declaring a settled analogy for AI-assisted engineering.

evidence.label: AI and the changing coding workflow

followups.question: How will new engineers develop judgment if AI performs many of the tasks that used to teach it?
answer: Novati calls this a difficult training problem. He favors education that alternates shorter academic periods with apprenticeships or internships, so learners gain experience with a mentor and real work. He points to co-op programs as one model and notes that employers, schools, and public support may need to share the cost. He also acknowledges that boot-camp graduates who already paid for training cannot simply rewind and choose a different path.

evidence.label: Apprenticeship and judgment

followups.question: What can a boot-camp graduate do when they have training but no engineering experience?
answer: He offers two nearer-term paths: look for a technology role that draws on an existing strength, then try to move toward engineering within that context; or build a small business or project with paying customers, whose feedback can develop product judgment. The larger answer remains uncertain: he believes practical apprenticeship is a better long-term bridge, but does not present it as an easy or established solution.

evidence.label: Two paths for a new entrant

blocks.question: Could a boot camp be structured like an apprenticeship?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati describes a small program that paired students with senior engineers doing paid client projects. Students watched experienced engineers work and some gradually contributed as contractors; he says several later found roles at Google. The model gave learners access to experience that classroom instruction alone could not provide.

He also explains why scaling it was difficult. Experienced engineers command high compensation elsewhere, and a program needs enough revenue to pay strong instructors. Boot camps that grow by having recent graduates teach newer students may struggle to transmit the taste and judgment that come from working beside someone substantially more experienced. Novati regards small-group mentorship as promising but says he does not know how far it scales.

evidence.label: A project-based apprenticeship model

blocks.question: Could a language model become a senior engineer?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati sees no inherent reason that a model could never do senior-level work. The obstacle, in his view at the time of recording, is access to information that is not public text: internal logs, metrics, hallway conversations, and context behind decisions. Senior engineers also make fewer but more consequential decisions, leaving less documented material for a model to learn from. He suggests that incident reviews could help teams learn from failure and become useful training material. He closes by arguing that people should be more open about mistakes, because judgment grows through seeing what went wrong and how a team responded.

evidence.label: Tacit knowledge, models, and learning from failure

blocks.question: Is the familiar coding-and-system-design interview a reasonable way to select engineers?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati calls the current format imperfect but not bad. A company could spend more time on each candidate or use a work trial, but those options bring cost, confidentiality, and intellectual-property concerns. He describes interview design as a practical engineering tradeoff: optimize for sufficiently accurate outcomes at scale, then use later performance processes to catch mismatches. He also notes that coding and algorithm problems sometimes do appear in real work, while acknowledging that interviews do not reproduce the job.

evidence.label: Interview design and practical tradeoffs

followups.question: What is a coding interview meant to measure?
answer: He says a well-run interview tries to remove language- and framework-specific advantages and observe how a candidate reasons, organizes code, and responds as constraints change. The interviewer is looking for the problem-solving process and the judgment behind the answer, not just a memorized optimal solution. He recognizes that an interview at scale may be delivered by someone who is not well trained, so execution can fall short of the intended design.

evidence.label: Reasoning over memorized answers

followups.question: What makes a system-design interview useful?
answer: Novati's aim as an interviewer was to have a grounded conversation about real systems and tradeoffs, not to pretend a candidate could design a full social network in 45 minutes and ship that design. He sees actual system design as more deliberate, nuanced, and often narrower in scope than the famous whiteboard prompt.

evidence.label: System design as a conversation

blocks.question: How should candidates prepare for interviews as AI enters the process?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati argues that the core preparation remains similar: candidates still need to communicate clearly, reason through a problem, and explain their choices. He says his company's before-and-after-AI preparation slides were the same because the underlying thinking process had not changed. A follow-up frames this as fluency rather than gamified memorization; Novati agrees with the emphasis on judgment, while noting that some interviews still suffer from inconsistent interviewer training.

evidence.label: Preparing for interviews in the AI era

followups.question: Do strong interviewers scale across large hiring processes?
answer: The host says skilled interviewers do not scale easily. Novati agrees that scaled processes produce variation and says that training matters; he has heard that Meta is trying to involve more senior engineers in interviewer training, though he explicitly says he has no inside information about the reason.

evidence.label: Interviewer quality at scale

blocks.question: What does Meta's newer AI-assisted coding interview look like, and is it likely to last?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati describes a practical exercise being added alongside classic whiteboard coding: candidates receive starter code in a limited coding environment, can use a simple language model, and work within a larger codebase to add features. He presents the format as an experiment that companies can calibrate against existing interviews, not an immediate full replacement.

Asked whether the shift is temporary, he predicts AI will remain part of interviews because engineers use it in daily work and employers need some signal about that skill. He expects the format and questions to keep changing, and says he has not yet heard enough detail to know exactly where the experiment will land.

evidence.label: AI-assisted interview experiments

blocks.question: Why might some highly valued engineers have little or no LinkedIn presence?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati describes a recruiting market where trusted recruiters maintain long-term relationships with senior engineers, so those engineers do not always need a public profile to hear about opportunities. He says some may keep only a minimal profile and cautions that this is not a reason for everyone to delete LinkedIn. His observation is about a narrow group of highly paid, established engineers, not a rule for early-career candidates.

evidence.label: Recruiting relationships and public profiles

followups.question: Does that mean engineers should avoid personal branding?
answer: No universal rule follows. Novati agrees that visible work can help earlier-career engineers, while he says many of the highest-paid current employees he has known did not build large public brands. He acknowledges exceptions and leaves room for generational differences, including younger engineers who have had a public presence from the start of their careers.

evidence.label: Personal brand and career stage

followups.question: Is the point simply that satisfied employees do not need to market themselves?
answer: The host offers that interpretation and Novati agrees, describing the job market as a kind of price discovery. He adds that his observation may fit older, established engineers better than people who have always built a public identity online.

evidence.label: Market fit and career stage

blocks.question: What current technology conversation does Novati think is overrated?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: He pushes back on claims that someone can produce a million-dollar software business in a weekend by vibe coding. Building a product is only one part of running a company; compliance, legal work, operations, and customer requirements can matter, especially for enterprise software. He does not want people to stop experimenting. His point is to keep the claims realistic and to focus on finding a strength that can create value rather than chasing a headline about money.

evidence.label: Vibe-coded companies and the work around software

followups.question: Why do million-dollar claims attract so much attention?
answer: The host suggests that people are drawn to the promised money more than to the software itself. Novati agrees and says that wealth does not automatically provide fulfillment: he has seen people keep chasing money or feel adrift when they have not built something useful. He argues that people benefit from earlier support in discovering and developing strengths, while recognizing that adults must work with the circumstances they have.

evidence.label: Money, fulfillment, and useful work

blocks.question: If AI makes individual developers more efficient, where will the gains go?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati does not claim to know. He contrasts a future where efficiency produces more goods and leisure with one where companies use AI to raise output expectations or displace jobs. He currently leans toward greater pressure to produce more, because fear of job loss may lead workers to use AI to expand output instead of taking more free time. He presents this as a concern and a forecast, not a settled outcome.

evidence.label: Who receives the gains from AI

blocks.question: Could your interview-preparation business fail to exist in five years?
blocks.speaker: Michael Novati
answer: Novati says that is possible. In his view, a business deserves to exist only while it creates value for customers. If AI changes what interview preparation requires, the company must adapt; if it can no longer help people, it should not continue merely for its own sake. He treats that possibility as part of building a company honestly.

evidence.label: Adapting a business to remain useful

sections.title: Multiply impact by growing capability and trusting people
sections.deck: The speaker distinguishes real leverage from working longer hours or splitting tasks, then shows how stretching people's skills and giving them room to act can increase a team's capacity.

blocks.heading: Leverage begins with skills
blocks.text: The speaker defines leverage as an input that produces greater output. An example contrasts two accountants who each handle twice the typical client load: one does so through a punishing 96-hour schedule, while the other learns Excel macros, Python, and automation. The point is not that effort is worthless; sustained hours can be a skill, but they are often unsustainable. Learning relevant capabilities can multiply output without relying on brute force.

evidence.label: The accountants and individual skill leverage

blocks.heading: Delegation can be only load balancing
blocks.text: After becoming a senior engineer, the speaker led a project with eight engineers. He carefully divided a hundred units of work among himself and junior and mid-level colleagues; the project finished on time and at high quality, yet his manager still asked him to improve at scaling through others. The reason was that the team had produced roughly the same hundred units of capacity that went in. Dividing a queue helps distribute effort, but it does not by itself develop the team or create leverage.

evidence.label: Project delegation and the manager's feedback

blocks.label: Stretch people just beyond their current ability
blocks.text: Force multiplication requires helping others acquire skills. Match a person with work they cannot quite do yet—whether the growth area is coding, design, or working with stakeholders—and provide the support needed to make the stretch manageable. The aim is not simply to offload a finished task; it is to increase what the person can handle next time.

evidence.label: Stretch assignments and skill development

blocks.heading: Trust is part of the mechanism
blocks.text: The speaker warns that daily check-ins and hovering can erase the capacity a leader hoped to gain. If a manager keeps solving the hard parts, the team member gets little practice and the leader's bandwidth stays consumed. Give people an appropriately sized scope, provide support and a safe context for growth, then step away enough for them to work through ambiguity. He recognizes that letting go is especially hard for strong performers who already know how to do the task themselves.

evidence.label: Micromanagement, trust, and autonomy

sections.title: Three career mistakes that compound
sections.deck: The speaker looks back on delayed investing, confusing task volume with impact, and staying on a team without examining whether it still supports growth.

blocks.heading: Mistake one: waiting too long to invest
blocks.text: The speaker recounts opening a retirement account early in his career, seeing it fall during the 2008 market crash, and selling at a loss. He says he then delayed investing for five or six years beyond an employer match. Using his own calculations, he estimates the missed gains at roughly $300,000 at the time of recording and projects a larger amount by retirement; those are his personal estimates, not guaranteed outcomes. His broader lesson is to start investing in some form when possible and value time in the market over attempts to time the market. He mentions retirement accounts, taxable investments, real estate, cryptocurrency, and investing in skills or a side business as examples, while not saying everyone should max out retirement accounts.

evidence.label: A delayed start to saving and investing

blocks.heading: Mistake two: counting output instead of impact
blocks.text: Early in his career, he equated taking more tickets, fixing more bugs, and writing more code with performing better. He later recognized that many routine tasks would have been handled by someone else and that doing 60 tickets rather than 45 may not distinguish an engineer if the additional volume does not matter. The alternative is to look for differentiated impact: prevent a recurring class of defects, identify a root cause, or improve a system in a way that changes outcomes. A role made entirely of routine upgrades can limit the opportunity to show judgment, so he advises seeking work where the quality and importance of the result can be visible.

evidence.label: Output versus differentiated impact

blocks.heading: Mistake three: deciding whether to stay by impulse
blocks.text: After working across many teams at Amazon, the speaker says he learned both to leave unhealthy situations and to avoid discarding a strong team for a marginal improvement. For an unclear case, he suggests examining the manager, pay relative to comparable roles, whether promised improvements are backed by action, and whether the work still offers learning and scope. He warns against believing verbal assurances when causes of attrition or operational problems remain unaddressed. He also describes staying too long on a team he liked even though it limited the scope needed for his next promotion. A team that is good can be hard to recognize until after it is gone, so he urges deliberate assessment rather than assuming the next option must be better.

evidence.label: When to leave a team
Manager and pay considerations
Promises backed by action
Growth, scope, and recognizing a good team

blocks.label: The three checks
blocks.text: Start investing when you can; ask whether your work changes an outcome; and evaluate team moves using concrete conditions such as management, pay, follow-through, and growth.

evidence.label: Investing
Impact
Team decisions

sections.title: Earn influence without giving up integrity
sections.deck: Ethan Evans explains how relationships, manager fit, transparent trade-offs, and visible business value shape promotions and day-to-day work.

blocks.question: What does corporate politics mean, and what should an engineer know about it?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: Evans uses politics to mean how people and organizations reconcile different goals and limited resources. That includes prioritizing competing products and deciding who receives a high-visibility project, a chance to step up, or access to senior leaders. It can become unethical, but the existence of politics does not require anyone to behave badly.

His first principle is to accept that relationships affect how work gets done. His second is to be reasonable rather than rigid or needlessly difficult. His third is that relationship skills and emotional intelligence are learnable; engineers can change how they deliver disagreement or bad news without abandoning technical standards.

evidence.label: A practical definition of workplace politics

followups.question: Does disengaging from politics protect an engineer from unethical behavior?
answer: The host adds that hierarchy and power dynamics matter, and Evans agrees that opting out does not stop other people from making decisions. Disengagement can leave an engineer without a voice or influence. Evans prefers to describe the subject as ordinary human relationships rather than a separate game.
followups.speaker: Host and Ethan Evans

evidence.label: Participation and power dynamics

blocks.question: How does Evans distinguish influence from manipulation?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: Evans starts with motive: influence tries to persuade someone toward an outcome believed to help them or the team, while manipulation primarily advances the persuader's interests. A transparent exchange can benefit both sides. For example, an employee might take on urgent work in exchange for a manager's commitment to advocate for the employee's contribution during calibration.

The same arrangement becomes manipulative if the employee invents complexity to secure headcount or undermines a colleague with selective evidence. Evans notes that ethical people can still lose a decision when someone else makes the stronger case.

evidence.label: Motive, mutual benefit, and manipulation

followups.question: How can an employee tell whether a decision process is becoming manipulative?
answer: Evans points to transparency and follow-through. If discussions happen in the open and commitments are kept, that supports trust; if plans repeatedly change behind closed doors, it is a reason to reassess. Taking an ethical, trusting approach may cost someone the first round, but they can learn from the mismatch between what was promised and what happened.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

evidence.label: Transparency and the first loss

followups.question: How can a candidate learn what a prospective manager is like?
answer: Evans recommends talking with people who have worked for that manager or company. He recalls a candidate who independently checked references with two former reports; both gave a clear warning, allowing the candidate to withdraw before accepting the job. He also tells employees to distinguish a manager's character from whether they personally like that manager's style.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

evidence.label: Reference checks and manager character

blocks.heading: A manager title does not guarantee management skill
blocks.text: The host points out that managers, like individual contributors, vary in performance. Evans separates competence gaps from ethics gaps: many managers receive little training, while some deliberately exploit their authority. Employees should not assume that a manager is automatically the adult in the room.

evidence.label: Manager skill and ethics

blocks.question: Why can an entire management chain share a blind spot?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: Evans calls this stacked flaws: a manager may fail to notice a weakness in a direct report when the manager shares the same weakness. He describes a period when he valued speed and bias for action, then hired similarly goal-driven managers. Other teams experienced them as wrecking balls, but Evans initially valued the results and did not see the damage.

Hiring people who resemble the manager can remove checks and balances, even when that feels easier in staff meetings. Employees can look at whether a skip-level leader resembles the direct manager, what behavior the organization rewards, and whether the employee is an outlier. Evans says people need to shop for a manager as deliberately as they shop for a role.

evidence.label: Stacked flaws and missing checks

blocks.question: When should someone try to repair a difficult manager relationship, and when should they pivot?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: Evans increasingly favors moving teams when a manager relationship is not working and a short attempt to improve it has failed. He suggests giving a new arrangement roughly three months, or six at most, to show a positive signal; employees should not let their lives disappear while waiting for a manager to change.

The host frames the test as an experiment: extend some trust, reflect on what went well, and perhaps give a second chance with more caution. A compelling project or promised promotion can make it harder to leave, but staying should be a conscious choice to accept the risk, not an assumption that effort will force an unethical manager to reward it.

evidence.label: Testing a difficult manager relationship

followups.question: What if an interesting project or a promised promotion makes it hard to leave?
answer: The host describes engineers who stay because they want to finish a meaningful project or believe a promise of greater scope will be honored. Evans says people can choose to accept that risk, but should recognize the likely cost in advance; otherwise, unfulfilled promises can leave them bitter about work they freely continued.
followups.speaker: Host and Ethan Evans

evidence.label: Project commitments and pre-accepting risk

blocks.question: What does it mean to manage up ethically?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: Evans calls managing up a legitimate skill. Employees and managers can discuss working styles, the information each needs, how they prefer feedback, and what should happen during an emergency. The goal is to find a working arrangement that gives the manager useful information while preserving the employee's room to do good work.

He uses a deliberately crude desk metaphor: employees can bring a manager an unsolved problem and leave it there, or remove a problem by solving it or proposing a clear next step. Managers tend to value the people who reduce uncertainty and make their work easier.

evidence.label: Discussing styles and reducing manager burden

blocks.text: The host adds that promotion requires someone in the management chain to advocate for the employee. Evans agrees that most engineers can find interesting technical work in many places, so an unsupportive manager is a reason to consider moving even when a project is compelling. He says people often overestimate how difficult job hunting will be, while his coaching clients who were forced to leave have frequently found better roles.

evidence.label: Manager sponsorship and changing jobs

blocks.question: How should a new employee avoid falling into order-taking mode?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: Instead of asking a manager to invent the employee's next task, Evans recommends learning the team's goals, surveying the work, and presenting a reasoned option: for example, explain the current commitments, identify several possible tasks, and recommend the one with the most value while inviting correction.

He calls the strongest version the magic loop: notice work that needs doing, handle it within the employee's judgment, and tell the manager what was done. He describes a client who spent half a day improving an internal tool; asking permission first created avoidable overhead, while completing the harmless improvement and reporting it demonstrated judgment. That autonomy depends on trust and a history of being right often enough.

evidence.label: From order taking to proactive work

followups.question: How much independence should a manager give before trust is established?
answer: Evans says autonomy grows through demonstrated judgment, not through a blanket rule. He recalls an engineer who rolled back another team's deployment without discussing it first; the team had to repair the relationship and recover from the tactical mistake. Once a manager knows an employee will use good judgment and communicate quickly when wrong, independent action becomes valuable.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

evidence.label: Trust and independent decisions

blocks.question: How should an employee respond when AI or other efficiency gains lead to an overloaded workload?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: Evans recommends presenting capacity as a shared prioritization problem. Explain what is already on the plate, identify the value of the work, and propose which lower-priority tasks could be stopped, automated, or reassigned so that higher-value work can fit.

Managers may not know what a task costs: a request that sounds like a small change can involve many hidden constraints. A clear account of time, dependencies, and trade-offs helps a reasonable manager understand the situation. Evans also notes that businesses accumulate zombie work, such as reports nobody reads, because teams rarely stop inherited tasks. If a manager dismisses the capacity evidence and insists that every task must be done, that is a useful signal about the relationship.

evidence.label: Capacity, priorities, and stale work

blocks.question: How can an employee discover what matters most to a manager?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: He offers several routes: read the manager's updates and all-hands messages, compare what teammates are working on, trace how the work connects to the company's business, and ask directly. Useful questions include what the manager's priorities are, what keeps them up at night, and whether an assigned task is the most important problem.

Evans says managers often carry an informal worry list and rarely receive offers of help. When an employee volunteers to handle a real concern, the manager has an incentive to provide the information and support needed to solve it. A useful offer can build a working relationship even when the two people do not especially like one another.

evidence.label: Finding a manager's priorities

blocks.question: How should an employee ask for a raise?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: Evans says the odds favor asking: he cites a survey in which about 30 percent of people ask for raises and roughly 70 percent of those who ask receive something, though not always the full amount requested. He advises opening with a reason rather than a bare demand. Strong reasons can include high performance, market or internal pay comparisons, and a true personal circumstance such as family needs.

The conversation should invite the manager to help make a case, not accuse them of withholding money. If the employee is already well paid, the argument needs to focus more on the value delivered; if the employee is doing good work while low in the salary band, fairness and room in the band can support the request.

evidence.label: Making a collaborative case for a raise

blocks.question: What is polite fiction at work, and when does it help or harm?
blocks.speaker: Ethan Evans
answer: Evans uses polite fiction for an accepted answer that smooths a social exchange, such as saying fine when someone casually asks how you are. It can also let a manager avoid forcing an employee to disclose that a doctor's appointment is really a job interview. Repeated signals may still require attention: several Friday appointments could suggest that an employee is interviewing or needs support.
He describes the term as a way people avoid difficult exchanges, not as proof that they should mislead one another.

evidence.label: Polite fiction and social smoothing

followups.question: When can polite fiction become a cover for manipulation?
answer: Evans says the boundary depends partly on how much trust and care exist in the relationship. Company policy can prevent a manager from disclosing a pending layoff or investigation, but he tries to be transparent when he can. He also says people who feel insecure or cornered are more likely to protect themselves with a lie; creating safety gives others a better chance to answer truthfully.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

evidence.label: Transparency, trust, and pressure

followups.question: Can a person preserve integrity without ever lying?
answer: Evans thinks complete truthfulness may be possible for someone secure enough to disclose difficult information, but he does not expect it from ordinary managers or employees. He distinguishes a socially smoothing or self-protective falsehood from a lie designed to advance one person at another's expense. The host adds that maturity also means recognizing when apparent harm was collateral damage rather than a personal attack.
followups.speaker: Host and Ethan Evans

evidence.label: Different kinds of lies and collateral damage

followups.question: What makes trust credible rather than just verbal?
answer: Evans says people earn trust by doing what they promised, especially when the promise costs them something. A teammate who accepts inconvenience or works through a difficult part of a partnership gives stronger evidence of commitment than someone who merely says the right thing.
followups.speaker: Ethan Evans

evidence.label: Trust shown through sacrifice
